claim: The phase of the neural signal aligns with temporal landmarks in both acoustic and linguistic dimensions during spoken language comprehension, a phenomenon referred to as neural tracking.
source: During this process, systematic changes shown by the acoustic signal are categorized by the brain as phonemes, while the similar ordering of consecutive phonemes creates words and, a certain ordering of words creates phrases and sentences. As these transformation occur, the phase of the neural signal is thought to align with temporal landmarks in both acoustic and linguistic dimensions; this phenomenon is referred to as neural tracking (Daube et al., 2019; Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Di Liberto et al., 2015; Brodbeck et al., 2018; Broderick et al., 2018; Daube et al., 2019; Keitel et al., 2018; Donhauser and Baillet, 2020; Gillis et al., 2021; Kaufeld et al., 2020a; Weissbart et al., 2020; Brodbeck et al., 2022; Heilbron et al., 2020; Coopmans et al., 2022; Slaats et al., 2023; Ten Oever et al., 2022a; Zioga et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Neural tracking has been proposed as a mechanism to segment the acoustic input into linguistic units such as phoneme, syllables, morphemes by aligning the neural excitability cycles to the incoming input.
source: Neural tracking has been proposed as a mechanism to segment the acoustic input into linguistic units such as phoneme, syllables, morphemes (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Ghitza, 2013; Ding et al., 2016) by aligning the neural excitability cycles to the incoming input.
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claim: Adding sub-lexical, lexical, and phrase- and sentence-level predictors to encoding models improves the reconstruction accuracy of neural responses on distinct sources in the brain.
source: Adding sub-lexical, lexical, and phrase- and sentence-level predictors, either quantified with information theoretic metrics (e.g. surprisal and entropy), or syntactic annotations, to the encoding model improves the reconstruction accuracy of neural responses on distinct sources in the brain (see Brodbeck et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Surprisal and entropy predictors have been shown to modulate the neural response at different time intervals.
source: surprisal and entropy predictors have been shown to modulate the neural response at different time intervals (see Donhauser and Baillet, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: During spoken language comprehension, acoustic, phonemic, phonological, and prosodic information is dynamically integrated with morphemic, lexical, semantic, and syntactic information.
source: During spoken language comprehension, acoustic, phonemic, phonological, and prosodic information is dynamically integrated with morphemic, lexical, semantic, and syntactic information (e.g., Bai et al., 2022; Kaufeld et al., 2020b; Kaufeld et al., 2020c; Marslen-Wilson and Welsh, 1978; Friederici, 2002; Hagoort, 2013; Martin et al., 2017; Oganian et al., 2023; Martin, 2016; Martin, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: In the Interactive Activation Model, feedback connections from word-level to phoneme-level enable a faster activation of phonemes in words than phonemes in nonwords.
source: In word recognition, models such as the Interactive Activation Model (McClelland and Rumelhart, 1981) and TRACE (Rumelhart and McClelland, 1982), feedback connections from word-level to phoneme-level enable a faster activation of phonemes in words than phonemes in nonwords by either enhancing the representation of expected phonemes or suppressing the competing phonemes.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical model

claim: Mispronounced or ambiguous phonemes are more likely to be missed by participants during a detection task when the context is more constraining.
source: It has also been demonstrated that mispronounced or ambiguous phonemes are more likely to be missed by participants during a detection task when the context is more constraining, indicating that top-down processing constraints interact with bottom-up sensory information to reduce the number of possible word candidates as the acoustic input unfolds (Marslen-Wilson and Welsh, 1978; Martin et al., 2017; Martin and Doumas, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: When the acoustic edges of the speech signal reach a threshold for the activation of a particular phoneme representation, the sensory representations of the acoustic edges are inhibited.
source: When the acoustic edges of the speech signal reach a threshold for the activation of a particular phoneme representation, the sensory representations of the acoustic edges are inhibited.
evidence: Based on theoretical model by Martin, 2016; Martin, 2020

claim: When context is less constraining, sub-lexical representations are less inhibited compared to in a highly constraining context.
source: According to this theoretical model, when context is less constraining, sub-lexical representations are less inhibited compared to in a highly constraining context.
evidence: Based on theoretical model by Martin, 2016; Martin, 2020

claim: It has been argued that neural tracking reflects the convolution of evoked responses to the change in acoustic envelope referred to as acoustic edges.
source: It has also been argued that neural tracking reflects the convolution of evoked responses to the change in acoustic envelope referred to as acoustic edges (Oganian et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Previous studies have shown that the intensity of the sound stimulus, and the constraints introduced on the words by the context of the sentence has an effect on the latency of the brain signal.
source: However, previous studies have shown that the intensity of the sound stimulus, and the constraints introduced on the words by the context of the sentence has an effect on the latency of the brain signal.

source: We collected MEG data from 24 participants between 18 and 58 years old (average age: 31.17 years, 18 F and 6 M)

source: They were all right handed native Dutch speakers with either no or very little French proficiency.

source: Brain activity of participants were recorded using magnetoencephalography (MEG) with a 275-sensor axial gradiometer system (CTF Systems Inc) in a magnetically shielded room.

claim: Modeling phoneme-level linguistic features in addition to acoustic features better reconstructs the neural tracking response to spoken language.
source: In this study, we show that modeling phoneme-level linguistic features in addition to acoustic features better reconstructs the neural tracking response to spoken language

claim: The improvement in reconstruction accuracy is even more pronounced in the comprehended language, likely reflecting the transformation of acoustic features into phoneme-level representations when a language is fully comprehended.
source: and that this improvement is even more pronounced in the comprehended language, likely reflecting the transformation of acoustic features into phoneme-level representations when a language is fully comprehended
evidence: Summary of main finding with interpretation

claim: Although acoustic edges are important for speech tracking, internally generated phonemes are more strongly encoded in comprehended language.
source: Although acoustic edges are important for speech tracking, internally generated phonemes are more strongly encoded in comprehended language.

claim: Low sentence- and discourse-level constraints enhanced the neural encoding of both acoustic and phoneme features.
source: We demonstrated that low sentence- and discourse-level constraints enhanced the neural encoding of both acoustic and phoneme features.

claim: When language is not comprehended, the neural encoding of acoustic features was stronger, likely due to the absence of comprehensive lexical access and interpretation.
source: When language is not comprehended, the neural encoding of acoustic features was stronger, likely due to the absence of comprehensive lexical access and interpretation, including higher level linguistic structure formation, in addition to the recognition of single, highly frequent function words (viz., the/a) in isolation.
evidence: Summary of main finding with interpretation

claim: Only in the comprehended language, phoneme features aligned with the phase of neural signal between 200 and 600ms, and this effect was stronger when the context was less constraining.
source: Only in the comprehended language, phoneme features aligned with the phase of neural signal between 200 and 600ms, and this is effect was stronger when the context was less constraining and more information must be extracted from the sensory signal.

claim: The persistence of phoneme-related neural activity before a word is recognized may reflect the time before phoneme-level information can be inhibited.
source: This pattern of results may reflect the persistence of phoneme-related neural activity before a word is recognized and phoneme-level information can be inhibited.

claim: The study used an MEG dataset of native Dutch speakers with no or minimal comprehension of French.
source: To this end, we made use of an MEG dataset of native Dutch speakers with no or minimal comprehension of French (i.e. self-report of no comprehension,<1 year education in French, chance performance on comprehension questions)

claim: The study used linear encoding modeling method to predict the MEG signal from acoustic and phoneme-level speech features.
source: We then used the linear encoding modeling method to predict the MEG signal from the acoustic and phoneme-level speech features including the spectrogram, acoustic edges, phoneme onset, phoneme surprisal and phoneme entropy

claim: Word entropy was used to quantify the sentence- and discourse-level constraint for each word given the preceding 30 words.
source: Word entropy was used to quantify the sentence- and discourse-level constraint for each word given the preceding 30 words.

claim: Phoneme surprisal quantifies the conditional probability of each phoneme in a word calculated according to the probability distribution over the lexicon weighted by the occurrence frequency of each word.
source: Phoneme surprisal quantifies the conditional probability of each phoneme in a word calculated according to the probability distribution over the lexicon weighted by the occurrence frequency of each word.

claim: Phoneme entropy reflects how constraining each phoneme is by quantifying the uncertainty about the next phoneme with each unfolding phoneme.
source: Phoneme entropy reflects how constraining each phoneme is by quantifying the uncertainty about the next phoneme with each unfolding phoneme.

claim: Contrasting a comprehended language with a language that is familiar, but not understood, allows separation of neural signals related to speech processing vs. those related to speech processing in the service of language comprehension.
source: Contrasting a comprehended language with a language that is familiar, but not understood, allows us to separate neural signals related to speech processing vs. those related to speech processing in the service of language comprehension.

claim: Having a high-familiarity, statistically known control language allows modeling the neural response to acoustic and phoneme-level features and contrasting it to a case where there is comprehension versus where there is not.
source: Having a high-familiarity, statistically known control language allows us to model the neural response to acoustic and phoneme-level features and contrast it to a case where there is comprehension versus where there is not.

claim: This is stronger control than examining the neural response to an unknown, statistically unfamiliar language, whose modulation of the neural response may mask the degree to which acoustic and phoneme-level processing dominate the neural signal during language comprehension.
source: This is stronger control than examining the neural response to an unknown, statistically unfamiliar language, whose modulation of the neural response may mask the degree to which acoustic and phoneme-level processing dominate the neural signal during language comprehension.
